doc.title: Sheila Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Middleburgh, New York, May 11, 2002

title: Rehearsing bass and voice: the freedom of a map
summary: Rehearsal gives a map for getting in and out of a tune, leaving freedom; she tells her bassists to lay out when in doubt.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: When you talk about rehearsing, how much does it affect the final performance?

It’s like — you know what? It’s like a map. Getting into it, knowing how to get into it, and knowing how to get out of it. And that’s it. The rest is pretty open. I mean nothing’s ever really set. There’s a lot of freedom with the bass and voice, a lot. So I love that. I love that freedom to be able to even go into another song if necessary. And I always say, as I did to Harvey or as I do to Cameron now, “Don’t try to follow me. If you don’t know the tune or if you don’t know where I’m going, just lay out. When in doubt, lay out.” And I’m on top of it. I’ll know when to bring it back in again. So the thing is having that freedom and having the other musician not be worried about whether or not — how are we going to get out of this, how did we get into it. So it’s just like really learning the tune. Just like you would teach your students, as I teach my students, learn the way it was written. Exactly the way it was written. Learn the tune the way it was written. What is the true melody of this tune?
